correctness.rationale: Uniqueness and permutation invariance of John/Löwner ellipsoids on irreducible sum-zero space force centered spheres. Ordered inequalities have normal Pi(e_i-c e_j), giving exact inradius; all are true facets. Every vertex has precisely two coordinate levels c/D_k and 1/D_k, including all nontrivial subsets (complete enumeration uses perturbation to exclude intermediate coordinates). Its norm squared is (c-1)^2 k(m-k)/(m(m+k(c-1))²). Writing q_k=(m-k)/k reduces the shell optimization to q_k/(c+q_k)²; pairwise equality occurs only at c=sqrt(q_i q_j), with adjacent geometric means decreasing, establishing no missed orbit/triple tie. Log derivatives of each candidate R_k/r have positive sign (m-2k)+(m-1-k)(c-1), establishing strict global ratio monotonicity. Independent shell-radii and geometric-mean transition checks in m=4,5,7,8 corroborated proof; end behavior and facet counts checked.

value.rationale: A natural continuous deformation of the trisected-simplex central polytope exhibits all outer ellipsoid contact orbit transitions, a rigid structural invariant with exact thresholds and a strict radius distortion interpolation. This moves beyond the known c=2 residue classification or the unrestricted-c vertex enumeration; no general external theorem is required for mathematical value.

final_claim: For m>=4 and real c>1, both John and Löwner ellipsoids of {sum x_i=1, x_i<=c x_j for all i!=j} in the regular-simplex Euclidean metric are barycentered balls. Their squared radii are the all-parameter facet-distance value and the maximum over two-level vertex shells; the exact outer contact shell switches at gamma_k=sqrt((m-k)(m-k-1)/(k(k+1))) (1<=k<floor(m/2)), with adjacent shell ties at each transition. Every facet touches the inner ball, and the outer/inner radius ratio increases strictly from sqrt(2 floor(m/2) ceil(m/2)/m) to m-1.
limitations: m>=4 and real c>1 in regular simplex metric. Euclidean radii do not persist numerically under arbitrary nonorthogonal affine changes; affine images of ellipsoids do.
